body:
We make Kiron, a workout app with a program built on this weekly structure. We're not affiliated with Andrew Huberman or the Huberman Lab podcast, and this isn't endorsed by them. The routine below comes from his podcast and newsletter (sources at the end).

Andrew Huberman, host of the Huberman Lab podcast, laid out his weekly workout routine in an October 2022 episode and a November 2022 newsletter, and he has updated it since. Here it is day by day, in our own words, with what changed and three ways to follow it.

His weekly schedule at a glance

As he described it in October and November 2022. He says the start day doesn't matter.
DayFocusWhat he does
Day 1, SundayLong, easy cardio60 to 75 minutes in Zone 2, usually a jog
Day 2, MondayLegsQuads, hamstrings and calves
Day 3, TuesdayHeat, cold and recoveryNo training; sauna and cold water
Day 4, WednesdayTorso and neckChest, back, shoulders and neck
Day 5, ThursdayModerate cardioAbout 35 minutes at 75 to 80 percent effort
Day 6, FridayIntervals8 to 12 rounds of 20 to 30 seconds all-out, 10 seconds rest
Day 7, SaturdayArms, calves and neckBiceps, triceps, calves and neck

Each muscle gets worked about twice a week: legs on Monday and again in Friday's intervals, and chest, back and shoulders on Wednesday and again through Saturday's dips and chin-ups.

The routine, day by day

Day 1 (Sunday): long, easy cardio

He aims for 60 to 75 minutes in Zone 2: breathing harder than normal, but still able to hold a conversation. He doesn't wear a heart rate monitor. He goes by that talk test, and on his own he breathes only through his nose. Usually it's a jog; rowing, cycling, swimming or a long hike, sometimes with a weight vest, work too. His weekly Zone 2 target is 180 to 200 minutes.

Day 2 (Monday): legs

About 10 minutes of warm-up, then 50 to 60 minutes of hard work, with two exercises per muscle: one that works it at full stretch, one that works it fully squeezed.

  • Quads: hack squat and leg extension. He uses the machine instead of barbell squats.
  • Hamstrings: glute-ham raise and leg curl. His newsletter offers straight-legged deadlifts in place of the raise.
  • Calves: standing and seated calf raises.

Sets are hard, with a struggle on the last reps, but not necessarily to failure.

The lifting rules: heavier and lighter months

His lifting alternates month by month: three to four weeks heavier, then three to four weeks lighter. He says staying heavy much past four weeks stalls his progress. His newsletter calls the two Schedule A and Schedule B:

From his newsletter and PDF, November 2022
Heavier month (A)Lighter month (B)
Reps per setAbout 4 to 8About 8 to 15
Sets per exercise3 to 42 to 3
Rest between sets2 to 4 minutesAbout 90 seconds

Sessions stay near an hour, 75 minutes at most, and only that long when he's waiting for equipment; he says longer ones hurt his recovery.

Day 3 (Tuesday): heat, cold and recovery

No running or lifting. His PDF describes 20 minutes in a sauna, then 5 minutes in an ice bath or cold shower, repeated three to five times, and says to start slowly. His newsletter adds that an ice bath shouldn't come straight after lifting: wait 6 to 8 hours, or do it before. By 2024 he called Tuesday a full rest day, with heat or cold optional.

We're reporting what he does, not recommending it. If you have a health condition, ask your doctor before trying either.

Day 4 (Wednesday): torso and neck

Pushing and pulling for the chest, back and shoulders. His PDF lists:

  • Chest: incline press and cable crossover.
  • Back: chin-ups or pull-ups, and a seated or dumbbell row.
  • Shoulders: shoulder press, lateral raises and rear-delt flies.

He sometimes alternates push and pull sets to save time. For his neck, he moves his head front to back and side to side against a light plate wrapped in a towel, aiming for a strong neck rather than a big one. He doesn't recommend neck bridges, and his PDF links a neck-training video.

Day 5 (Thursday): moderate cardio

After a 5 to 10 minute warm-up, he goes 30 to 35 minutes at a steady 75 to 80 percent of all-out, hard enough that he can't keep to nose breathing. He usually runs; a rower, bike, stairs or jump rope work too.

Day 6 (Friday): intervals

His first choice is an air bike (the kind with moving handles and a fan): 20 to 30 seconds all-out with arms and legs, 10 seconds of rest, for 8 to 12 rounds, trying to get near his maximum heart rate. A rower, ski machine or sprint-and-jog intervals work too. His rule is to go all-out only on a movement you can do with perfect form, so he holds running sprints to about 95 percent.

Day 7 (Saturday): arms, calves and neck

  • Biceps: incline curls, dumbbell curls, and two or three sets of palms-facing chin-ups.
  • Triceps: overhead extensions or kickbacks, plus dips.
  • Calves: standing and seated raises again, and his PDF adds tibialis raises for the front of the shin.
  • Neck: as on Wednesday.

Moving days around

Any session can slide a day earlier or later, a missed one can be doubled up later in the week, and he sometimes swaps Wednesday and Thursday. The spacing rule he keeps: no hard intervals the day after legs. For more on fitting runs around lifting, see our guide to running and lifting in the same week.

How the routine has changed since 2022

He has revisited the week on the podcast since:

2022: his Fitness Toolkit episode and newsletter PDF. 2023: his Science-Supported Tools episode. 2024: AMA #17.
In 2022Later
Week startsSunday, with the long cardio2024: Monday, with legs, on the same weekdays
TuesdaySauna and cold2024: full rest; heat or cold optional
Moderate run30 to 35 minutes at 75 to 80 percent2023: 25 to 30 minutes. 2024: 20 to 30, a bit faster than Zone 2
Intervals20 to 30 seconds hard, 8 to 12 rounds2024: about 20 seconds hard, about 8 rounds
Long session60 to 75 minute jog, or a long hike2023: 60 to 90 minute jog, or a 1 to 4 hour hike. 2024: a weighted hike, or a walk with a loaded pack
Heavy lifting4 to 8 reps, every other month2023: 12 weeks of 3 to 5 reps, a scheme from exercise scientist Andy Galpin, then mostly 6 to 10

In 2024 he also added tibialis work to leg day and abs to Saturday. Even the 2022 sources differ a little: the PDF allows intervals of up to 60 seconds, and the newsletter says he never trains chest directly, getting that work from dips.

Three ways to follow it

A printout and a notebook

Print the PDF from his newsletter page and log each session in a notebook. It's free. The catch is the bookkeeping: you choose the weights, track which month you're in and build up the cardio yourself.

Any workout log

Set up the three lifting days as routines in the log you already use, and change the sets and reps by hand each month. Three routines fit in the free plans of logs like Hevy and Strong. Our guide to workout apps for following a program compares them.

Kiron's 7-Day Longevity Protocol

Kiron (that's us) is a workout app for {{kiron:cell-platforms}}. Its 7-Day Longevity Protocol, one of {{kiron:program-count}} ready-made programs, is built on this weekly structure and does the bookkeeping for you:

  • 16 weeks of alternating four-week phases, moderate, heavy, moderate, heavy. Moderate phases use mostly 8 to 15 reps with shorter rests; heavy phases mostly 6 to 8, with rests up to 3 minutes.
  • The exercises he names, in his stretched-and-squeezed pairs, the same every week: hack squat, leg extension, leg curl, glute-ham raise, calf and tibialis raises, incline dumbbell press, cable crossover, pull-ups, seated row, shoulder press, lateral raises, rear-delt flies, dips, curls, overhead triceps extensions and chin-ups.
  • Weights suggested from your history, with a short note on why, such as what you last lifted or a related lift you've logged. After each set it asks how the weight felt and adjusts the rest, and your weights go up as you get stronger.
  • Cardio that builds each phase: Sunday's long run grows from 45 to 75 minutes, Thursday's tempo run from 25 to 35, and Friday's air-bike sprints from 8 to 12 rounds of 20 seconds hard, 10 easy.
  • Fixed days, from Monday's legs to Sunday's long run. Move or skip a missed workout, or start one a day early. If set days don't suit your week, choose Whenever I train, and the workouts wait for you in order.
  • {{kiron:offline-lead}} {{kiron:offline-detail}}

Where it differs from his version:

  • Neck: Kiron has no weighted neck exercise, so chin tucks, with no weight, stand in for his plate and towel.
  • It starts with a moderate phase, to ease you into six days a week and let your suggested weights settle. His sources describe the heavy month first.
  • No sauna or cold. Tuesday is a rest day, as in his 2024 week.
  • The air bike is the sprint machine, though the notes say a rower or ski machine works too. Sprints are 20 seconds, the short end of his range.
  • Smaller things: each week runs Monday to Sunday, so the long run closes it, and that run starts at 45 minutes. Heavy phases stop at 6 reps rather than 4, and there are no abs.

You'll need a gym with machines, cables, dumbbells, an air bike, and pull-up and dip bars. It's built for people who already lift and can run for 30 minutes.

{{kiron:pricing-sentence}}

Prefer his 2024 week, or your own version? Paste it in as text, and Kiron turns it into a program on your calendar.

Quick answers

Is there a Huberman workout PDF?

Yes. His November 2, 2022 newsletter, Foundational Fitness Protocol, links to a free one-page PDF. We don't host a copy. It's the 2022 version, without the later changes.

How many days a week is it?

Six training days and one recovery day: a split of three lifting days (legs; torso and neck; arms, calves and neck) and three cardio days. In 2024 he said he aims to make 85 to 95 percent of his workouts, not all of them.

How long are the workouts?

Lifting days are about 10 minutes of warm-up and 50 to 60 of work, 75 at most. Cardio runs from an interval session of 8 to 15 minutes in all (his 2024 count) to an hour or more on Sunday.

What does Zone 2 mean?

Easy, steady cardio: breathing harder than normal but still able to talk. Many watches define it by heart rate, but he goes by the talk test, and in 2023 he offered another check: a pace you can hold breathing only through your nose.

Is it good for beginners?

It's a lot to start with: six days a week, a long run and all-out intervals. He suggests newcomers start the long session shorter and on flat ground, and starting with fewer days helps too. Kiron's version is for people who already lift; its First Month in the Gym and Beginner 5K are gentler starts. If you have a health condition, check with your doctor before starting.

If you want this week without the bookkeeping, try Kiron's 7-Day Longevity Protocol. {{kiron:cta-sentence}} Get Kiron.

If you'd rather not pay for an app, his PDF and a notebook will do the job.
